articles.title: What the spec map is
articles.summary: Every paint file comes with a second picture, the spec map, a separate texture file that tells iRacing how shiny, how metallic and how rough each spot of the car is (see colour space and files).
articles.what: The colour file says what colour each spot is. The spec map says what each spot is made of. Four values per pixel carry that: R for metallic, G for roughness, B for clearcoat and A for the lighting mask. The paint can be a perfect red and still look like cheap plastic if the spec map is wrong, and the reverse is just as true. Shokker Paint Booth builds both files for you, one pair per car, at 2048 by 2048 pixels covering the whole car laid flat.
when: You wonder why two paints with the same colour look different on track
You want a chrome, a matte or a candy look and need to know what is really changing
You are about to touch any SPEC slider and want to know what it does
how: Pick a finish for a zone. The finish already carries its own spec values.
Look at the finish card or use the Spec Map Inspector to see its R, G and B numbers.
Move SPEC STRENGTH or the R METAL, G ROUGH and B COAT sliders to push the look.
Render. The paint and the spec map are written together.

pitfalls: A spec map is not a second colour image. Do not expect it to show colour on the car.

deep.heading: How iRacing reads the two pictures
deep.body: iRacing gets two pictures for your car. The paint picture is the colour you see. The spec picture is four numbers per pixel that tell the lighting engine what the surface is made of: red is metal, green is roughness, blue is the clear layer on top, alpha is a lighting mask. The sim lights every pixel from those four numbers, using its sun, sky and your view angle. That is why the same paint can look like wet enamel, brushed steel or flat vinyl without a single colour changing.

deep.heading: Why paint and spec are never judged apart
deep.body: Metal reflection is tinted by the paint colour, while clear-coat highlights are close to white. So a metal value of 255 on a near-white paint gives silver, the same value on a dark red gives dark tinted metal, and on near-black it can vanish. The spec only decides how much of each effect you get. The colour you painted decides what that effect looks like. Judge the two together, on the car, never one without the other.

deep.heading: What Shokker Paint Booth does for you
deep.body: You never paint these four numbers by hand. Every zone has a base finish that sets a starting metal, roughness and coat, then pattern, overlays and sliders move them. At the very end the app raises any coat value below 16 to 16 and any roughness below 15 to 15 unless the pixel is chrome tier (metal 240 or more), so a render cannot hand iRacing a value that whitewashes. The paint goes out as a 24-bit picture and the spec as a 32-bit picture with alpha, both for the same car.

faq.q: Do I have to understand the spec map to use the app?
faq.a: No. Pick a finish and the app sets all four numbers. Read this when you want to tune a shine, fix a washed-out look or build your own material.

faq.q: Does the spec map change how the car drives?
faq.a: No. Spec only changes how the car looks, never how it handles.

faq.q: What happens if there is no spec file?
faq.a: iRacing falls back to the car's normal material and your colours still show. You just lose your custom shine.

faq.q: Why does iRacing look different from the preview?
faq.a: The preview is a quick design view. iRacing lights the real render with its own sun, shadows and materials, and it reads the spec file separately, so shine only shows in the sim.

faq.q: Do I need to understand spec to make a good paint?
faq.a: No. Pick a finish and the app sets all four numbers; a first paint needs only a template, a zone, a finish and RENDER. Knowing the spec helps when you want to tune a shine or fix a washed-out look.

faq.q: Do I have to learn the spec map before my paint can look good?
faq.a: No. The defaults and finishes handle the shine for you; knowing the spec map only helps when you want finer control. For a first paint, pick a finish and render.

faq.q: Is the spec map a transparency channel or an independent image?
faq.a: An independent image: the second picture, a separate texture file next to your paint, not paint transparency. Its alpha is only the lighting mask, and iRacing reads it for metal, roughness and clearcoat (see colour space and files).

mistakes.symptom: The finish looks washed out and white in the sim.
mistakes.cause: A clear-coat value between 1 and 15 reached iRacing. That band is treated as no coat or a legacy value.
mistakes.fix: Re-render from the app instead of editing the file by hand. The app raises every coat value to at least 16.

mistakes.symptom: Silver chrome comes out black or grey.
mistakes.cause: Metal reflection takes the paint colour, and the paint under it was dark or mid grey.
mistakes.fix: Paint the zone near-white, or use a Foundation chrome with Use source paint if you want to keep your colours and accept tinted chrome.

mistakes.symptom: I changed a spec value and nothing happened.
mistakes.cause: The old compiled copy of the spec is still loaded by the sim.
mistakes.fix: Render again, then press Ctrl+R in iRacing. If it still looks old, move the compiled spec copy for that car out of the folder and reload.

protips: The preview shows the same colours as the render but not the same shine, so judge shine on the spec views (R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT) and in the sim.
A dark paint under high metal is buried: nearly black until the right reflection arrives. Colour first, then metal.

articles.title: R channel: metallic
articles.summary: Red stores metallic, independently from green roughness and blue clearcoat. Ordinary SPB output below metallic 240 floors roughness at 15; at 240 or above that non-chrome floor no longer applies. Metallic alone does not guarantee a mirror or a drawn texture.
articles.what: The metallic channel describes the material response, not decorative red paint. The registered plain Foundation Pearl starts at M/R/CC 100/40/16, Metallic at 200/50/16 and Chrome at 255/2/16. These are individual starting material registrations, not universal bands that classify every finish or exported pixel. The reviewed plain Metallic base draws no flakes. Roughness, clearcoat, strength, masks and overlays remain separate factors, and reflected appearance must be checked in the intended viewing conditions.

You are choosing between pearl, metallic and chrome
how: Open the zone editor, go to the BASE section and find Spec Sliders.
Move R METAL right to add metal or left to remove it. Each tick is 5.

deep.heading: Threshold versus material identity
deep.body: The code threshold at metallic240 decides ordinary roughness flooring. It does not certify that the finish looks like chrome, and it does not identify a drawn texture or the biological/material construction of a finish.

faq.q: What changes between metallic 239 and 240 for roughness?
faq.a: In ordinary SPB output, metallic 239 is below the chrome threshold and roughness is floored at 15. At metallic 240, that non-chrome floor no longer applies. Explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels are a separate roughness exception; authored clearcoat preservation alone is not.

faq.q: Can roughness two survive at metallic 239 instead of 240?
faq.a: In ordinary output, metallic 239 with roughness 2 becomes roughness 15. Metallic 240 can retain roughness 2. Explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels can bypass the final roughness floor, so check the selected path and composed map.

faq.q: Does high metallic always make a perfect mirror?
faq.a: Metallic alone does not guarantee a mirror appearance. Inspect roughness, clearcoat, strength, overlays, the intended target and viewing conditions. Plain Foundation Chrome starts at 255/2/16, but that is a registered comparison point, not universal appearance acceptance.

faq.q: Does plain Foundation Metallic add metal flakes?
faq.a: No. The reviewed plain Foundation Metallic base has constant starting M/R/CC 200/50/16 and draws no grain or flakes. Texture is a separate choice.

faq.q: Can plain glossy paint have zero metallic?
faq.a: Yes. Plain Foundation Gloss starts at M/R/CC 0/30/16. Nonmetal gloss is valid; do not diagnose a black metallic channel as a fault by itself.

faq.q: Does metal200 describe a physical percentage of metal in the car?
faq.a: No. An actual metallic byte200 is an encoded material value, not physical material composition or a guaranteed reflected appearance.

faq.q: If I swap red and green spec channel bytes, am I swapping paint colours or material properties?
faq.a: You would change the material encoding: red bytes supply metallic and green bytes supply roughness. This is not exchanging red and green decorative paint. It can produce a very different material response, and final output constraints may modify values. This explanation does not claim an Offline command exists to perform a spec-channel swap.

articles.title: G channel: roughness
articles.summary: Green stores roughness: lower values describe a smoother underlying material and higher values a rougher one. Ordinary SPB output floors roughness at 15 below metal 240; explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels are an exception.
articles.what: Roughness and metallic are separate material channels; clearcoat has its own blue channel. Inspect the combined spec rather than reading appearance from roughness alone. In the inspected ordinary output, metal below 240 keeps roughness at least 15. Metal 240 or greater can retain lower roughness, and explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels bypass this final roughness floor. Recognized authored clearcoat preservation by itself does not bypass roughness flooring. A lower roughness number is not a guarantee of perfect mirror appearance in every light, car or composed material.

You want to go from gloss to satin to matte
how: Inspect the G ROUGH channel and the actual intended material target.
Compare the combined metallic, roughness and clearcoat channels, together with strength and overlays.

controls.label: G ROUGH
controls.effect: Adds or removes roughness on top of the finish.

tips: Compare one material change at a time.
A registered base number is a starting point; overlays and strength can change the composed result.
pitfalls: Do not call every low-green pixel chrome; metallic and clearcoat are separate channels.
Do not infer visible porosity, grain or flakes from a roughness band alone.
A clearcoat preservation exception is not automatically a roughness exception.

deep.heading: Ordinary floor and selected exceptions
deep.body: Ordinary SPB output floors roughness below15 when metallic is below240. The inspected final output exempts explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels. Clearcoat preservation is a different condition and does not grant a roughness exception.

deep.heading: Registered starting points, not fixed appearance bands
deep.body: Plain Foundation Gloss starts at M/R/CC 0/30/16, Matte at 0/200/160 and Chrome at 255/2/16. These registered base values are useful comparisons, not final composed pixel values, native appearance endorsements or proof of texture.

faq.q: What roughness is a mirror?
faq.a: A low roughness value describes a smooth material, but does not guarantee a perfect reflected appearance. Plain Foundation Chrome starts at M/R/CC 255/2/16. Ordinary nonmetal output is floored at roughness 15; inspect the full composed material and viewing conditions.

faq.q: Why can I not go below 15 on a gloss car?
faq.a: In ordinary output, metal below 240 floors roughness at 15. Explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels bypass this final floor. Recognized authored clearcoat preservation alone does not bypass roughness flooring.

faq.q: Does roughness change the colour?
faq.a: Roughness is a material channel, not decorative paint RGB. A different material response can change apparent colour under reflections even when source paint is retained. Other paint contributors still need inspection.

faq.q: Do imported clearcoat values allow roughness below 15?
faq.a: Not automatically. Mere import does not establish preservation. Even recognized authored clearcoat preservation does not itself bypass roughness flooring; the inspected roughness exception is explicitly preserved pattern spec.

faq.q: Is the roughness floor applied on every pixel of every render?
faq.a: No universal claim is safe. The inspected ordinary final output floors non-chrome pixels, except explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels. Metal 240 or above can retain roughness below 15. Check the exact composed path and selected source.

faq.q: Is roughness50 the same as fifty percent glossy?
faq.a: No. An actual8-bit roughness value50 is not fifty percent gloss. Distinguish raw channel bytes, percentage controls and Offline shorthand; the final roughness map depends on the composed material path.

faq.q: Does roughness flip the red and white paint colours?
faq.a: Roughness is encoded in the green spec channel. It changes material response rather than exchanging red and white decorative paint RGB. Reflected appearance can change without RGB repainting. COLOR FLIP is a separate colour treatment; a roughness value is not a paint-colour swap command.

faq.q: Can increasing roughness change the reflected appearance without repainting RGB?
faq.a: Yes. Roughness controls material response separately from decorative RGB. The apparent colour and reflections can change even when source paint pixels are retained. Check paint and spec separately and inspect other contributors before concluding the final composition preserves artwork.

mistakes.symptom: A low roughness value survives despite the ordinary floor
mistakes.cause: The pixel may be chrome-tier or explicitly preserved pattern spec; inspect the exact path before diagnosing a bug
mistakes.fix: Check composed metallic and preservation ownership, not just the green input value.

mistakes.symptom: A roughness change does not produce the intended appearance
mistakes.cause: Metallic, clearcoat, strength, overlays, target and viewing conditions also affect the result
mistakes.fix: Inspect the full composed material and change one factor at a time. Do not assume a universal roughness band guarantees the appearance.

articles.title: B channel: clearcoat (it runs backwards)
articles.summary: Blue stores clearcoat material data, not blue paint. In SPB,16 is the glossy clearcoat end; larger values weaken that response. Normal final rendering floors blue to16 but permits255. Authored-spec and pattern-spec preservation have explicit exceptions.
articles.what: Treat the spec picture as channel data: red is metallic, green is roughness and blue is clearcoat. Its combined RGB colours are not the visible paint colour. In SPB clearcoat conventions,16 is the strongest glossy coat and values toward255 weaken it; exact0 is an authored no-coat case. The normal final output raises blue values below16 to16, not values above254 down to254:255 is allowed. Pixels flagged for authored-spec or pattern-spec preservation bypass that lower floor. The authored exception is tied to a recognized authored-spec finish and its owned pixels, not merely to any file you import. Other material passes, overlays, blends and adjustments can affect final output. Use the actual rendered spec and the sim lighting to judge the result; a blue slider value alone does not describe overall matte or gloss.
when: You want a wetter or a drier top layer
A finish looks washed out and you suspect the coat value
how: Select the intended zone and inspect its actual artwork/layer coverage.

Use B COAT in Spec Sliders to adjust the clearcoat channel. Lower effective values toward16 for a stronger coat; raise them for weaker clearcoat response. The slider is an offset, not the final exported blue value.
Check G ROUGH as well: roughness controls the surface response separately. Raising blue alone does not guarantee a matte-looking car.
Inspect the rendered B COAT channel or spec output after all effects. Normal output keeps values within0..255 and applies the lower16floor except recognized preservation pixels.
If authored or pattern spec is involved, check the specific import/mode and final output rather than assuming the ordinary lower-floor rule applies everywhere.

deep.heading: The backwards channel in full
deep.body: Blue 16 is the strongest active coat. Values rise toward 255 as the coat fades: 17 to 31 very strong, 32 to 63 strong to medium, 64 to 127 satin, 128 to 191 dull, 192 to 254 almost none, 255 none. Values 0 to 15 are treated by the sim as no coat or a legacy value. 255 is the raw maximum byte but the weakest clearcoat. Old notes that call it maximum are wrong.

deep.heading: The floor of 16 and its two exceptions
deep.body: In a normal render every coat value is raised to at least 16, including matte, so no pixel lands in the 1 to 15 band that whitewashes. The two exceptions are pixels from an imported spec (including the SHOKK DROP authored sets) and pixels where a pattern spec amount is on; those keep their exact values, 0 included. Resizing or smoothing a spec picture can create 1 to 15 values by accident, which is another reason to re-render instead of resizing.

deep.heading: Clearcoat quality and strength
deep.body: The quality control maps straight onto the byte: coat = 16 + (1 minus quality) times 239. Quality 1.0 is coat 16, quality 0.5 is about 135, quality 0 is 255. Spec Strength pulls coat toward 16: coat becomes 16 + (coat minus 16) times strength, so strength 0 gives the full glossy 16. Never blend a coat value from 0 to 16 across an edge; the blend passes through the dead 1 to 15 band. Use a hard edge or blend from 16 upward.

deep.heading: Ordinary output and deliberate no-coat data
deep.body: Normal output raises clearcoat values below16 to16 while allowing values up to255. Recognized authored-spec pixels and explicit pattern-spec preservation can bypass the lower floor. This is not a guarantee for every import mode or every later material effect. Inspect the completed spec output when preserving deliberate no-coat data is important.

faq.q: Is a bigger blue number more clearcoat?
faq.a: No. It is the reverse. 16 is the strongest coat and 255 is none.

faq.q: Why does the app raise my coat 0 to 16?
faq.a: The normal final render applies a lower clearcoat floor of16. Recognized authored-spec and pattern-spec preservation pixels bypass it. Merely importing a file is not enough to establish that exception; inspect the actual finish/mode and final spec.

faq.q: What coat do Foundation finishes use?
faq.a: Gloss and Wet Look 16, Pearl 16, Metallic 16, Chrome 16, Candy 16, Satin Chrome 40, Satin 70, Brushed 65, Matte 160.

faq.q: Can I make blue 255 for a matte look?
faq.a: Yes, normal final spec output allows255; it is not restricted to imported specs. Blue255 weakens clearcoat response, but does not by itself guarantee a matte appearance. Choose suitable roughness and material values as well and check the finished spec and sim.

faq.q: What is clearcoat and why does a car need it?
faq.a: Clearcoat is represented by the blue material channel, separate from paint colour. In SPB,16 is the glossy clearcoat end and larger values weaken that response. It works together with metallic and roughness; matte or gloss is not determined by blue alone.

faq.q: Does blue in my spec map make the car blue?
faq.a: No. The blue channel stores clearcoat data. The visible paint colour comes from the paint output; a spec map displayed as RGB can look colourful without being the car paint.

faq.q: Does increasing B COAT make the car shinier?
faq.a: No. A higher effective blue value weakens clearcoat response; lowering it toward16 gives the stronger coat. Check roughness and metal too, because these channels jointly affect the reflected appearance.

faq.q: Can normal SPB output contain clearcoat255?
faq.a: Yes. The normal final uint8spec conversion clips to0..255, and its ordinary clearcoat rule is a lower floor of16. It does not ban255 or require an imported spec to reach it.

faq.q: Is the B COAT slider the blue value in the exported spec?
faq.a: No. B COAT is an adjustment to the material channel. The base, patterns, overlays, blends, other controls and final render rules determine the exported value. Inspect the completed spec rather than equating slider0 with exported blue0.

faq.q: Will any imported spec preserve blue0?
faq.a: Do not assume that. The final lower-floor exception is tied to recognized authored-spec ownership and explicit pattern-spec preservation. The specific import/mode matters. Check the actual final output before promising byte-preserved blue0.

faq.q: Why is my car still shiny with high clearcoat blue?
faq.a: Clearcoat is only one part of the material response. Check roughness and metallic values, the zone coverage, competing effects and the actual rendered spec. High blue weakens the clearcoat response but is not a guarantee of an overall matte appearance.

faq.q: Can I get blue255 without importing a spec?
faq.a: Yes. Normal final spec output permits blue255. It applies a lower clearcoat floor of16, not a maximum of254. A weak clearcoat response alone does not guarantee a matte appearance: inspect roughness and metallic too.

faq.q: An iRacing guide says the blue spec channel is unused. Is that still the right guidance?
faq.a: That describes the older setup. The official Paint Textures article is dated December 2019; the December 2022 release notes for2023 Season 1 explicitly introduced blue-channel clearcoat. Use the newer channel meaning when reading SPB's B COAT controls. SPB's ordinary clearcoat floor and preservation exceptions are separate application behavior.

faq.q: My combined spec preview is blue over a red sponsor; is the sponsor now blue?
faq.a: Blue in combined spec encodes clearcoat. Decorative paint RGB is a separate image, although a changed material can alter perceived appearance. Encoded preview colour is not the decorative palette.

articles.title: A channel: the lighting mask
articles.summary: Spec alpha is material-lighting data, not diffuse paint transparency, geometry or emission. The general imported RGB map initializer supplies alpha 255 because RGB has no authored alpha; RGBA initially retains it. Use Source Alpha removes the Zone override and retains incoming alpha, which need not be 255. Final output and simulator appearance need checking.
articles.what: The official2019 iRacing guide describes spec alpha as masking reflection/specular effects. That historical description does not establish that A0 removes every current lighting component, A128 halves visible brightness, or that every car responds identically. SPB’s current zone helper copies an RGBA spec and replaces only its alpha with the rounded/clamped override; source/no override leaves the incoming alpha unchanged. This helper and the actual32-bit TGA writer passed ten synthetic array round trips with RGB and source arrays unchanged. No full live endpoint render or simulator lighting was executed.
when: You are making an unlit shape such as a fake hole or a glowing decal
You want to flatten shine over a sponsor area
how: Identify the intended Zone and its selected footprint before applying a mask; locked Intensity blocks the preset UI change.
Choose Use Source Alpha to remove the override, or an explicit255/128/0 preset when an alpha override is intended. Source is not synonymous with255.
Inspect the resulting alpha and material output. The override changes alpha, not the underlying RGB material values in the reviewed helper.
Use roughness/clearcoat for material finish decisions and keep alpha experiments separate; verify the actual simulator response.
tips: Keep normal body paint at 255.
The edge between zones blends alpha as well as colour, so a soft edge gives a soft lighting fade.
pitfalls: Alpha 0 over a big area makes the car look like a flat sticker on track.
Alpha stays at 255 unless you set a lighting mask or override, so do not expect holes you did not make.

deep.heading: Local override versus perceived lighting
deep.body: The helper accepts finite numeric overrides, rounds and clamps to0–255, copies RGBA input and replaces channel3 only. Missing/empty/invalid overrides leave the source unchanged. Local presets label these values Full/Reduced/Kill Lighting, but those labels are not measured brightness or all-lighting contracts.

deep.heading: Zone boundaries are not a universal smooth fade
deep.body: In the reviewed ordinary car composition branch hard edges use mask>=.5 ownership. Soft edges replace with the zone result above.5, blend only for.05<mask<=.5, and leave lower coverage unchanged. Alpha follows this channel-wise composition; do not promise a continuous fade across the entire mask.

deep.heading: Source and export limits
deep.body: Use Source Alpha removes the explicit override rather than resetting to255. Current JS serialization and server sanitization carry the value to the zone helper; the car spec path calls the32-bit writer. Synthetic helper/writer round trips prove local byte preservation, not full endpoint behavior with later material/wear contributors or simulator acceptance.

faq.q: Should I touch alpha for a normal car?
faq.a: Use the template/source alpha unless you have an intentional reason to override it. Full Lighting explicitly writes255; Use Source Alpha removes the override and can retain a different incoming value.

faq.q: Can alpha make a hole in the car?
faq.a: It can mask reflection/specular effects according to historical iRacing documentation, but it does not cut geometry or make paint transparent. Inspect the exact car/template and simulator result.

faq.q: Why does my matte look flat and dead?
faq.a: Check whether you changed alpha as well as materials. Do not diagnose alpha from appearance alone. Restore the intended source alpha or deliberate255 override, then inspect roughness/clearcoat and actual lighting separately.

faq.q: Does soft edge affect alpha?
faq.a: In the reviewed ordinary car branch alpha composes with the other channels: hard masks use majority ownership; soft masks replace above.5, blend only between.05 and.5, and leave lower coverage unchanged. This is not a continuous fade across the entire mask.

faq.q: Does the spec A channel matter in iRacing?
faq.a: Spec alpha is a material-lighting mask, not paint transparency, geometry or an emission source. SPB presets write A255/A128/A0; Use Source Alpha removes the override and retains the incoming zone spec alpha, which need not be255. The exact simulator appearance needs checking.

faq.q: Does Use Source Alpha always reset alpha to255?
faq.a: No. It removes the explicit override. The reviewed zone helper leaves the incoming spec alpha unchanged when no valid override is supplied; imported or authored source values may differ from255.

faq.q: Does A128 guarantee half the visible brightness?
faq.a: No visible-brightness measurement was established. A128 is the app’s numeric preset. The simulator’s shader and lighting determine its appearance; the historical guide describes masking reflection/specular effects.

faq.q: When I remove the alpha override can my imported spec values stay?
faq.a: Removing only the lighting-mask override leaves incoming alpha unchanged in the reviewed zone helper. Imported values can remain, but material remaps/overrides, later contributors and final composition are separate checks. It is not a reset to255 and does not undo unrelated edits.

faq.q: Will the lighting mask erase my paint or cut a real vent?
faq.a: No. The reviewed helper replaces only spec alpha; RGB material channels and the original array stay unchanged. It does not cut car geometry or erase paint. Historical iRacing guidance describes masking reflection/specular effects; verify actual simulator behavior.

faq.q: Is reduced lighting exactly fifty percent as bright on all cars?
faq.a: No such brightness guarantee was measured. Reduced Lighting writes alpha128, while Spec Strength is a different control for M/R/C. The simulator’s lighting/material response determines perceived brightness; a numeric midpoint does not prove half the visible brightness.

mistakes.symptom: Source Alpha did not become255.
mistakes.cause: Source removes the override; it is not a forced255 preset.
mistakes.fix: Inspect incoming alpha or choose Full Lighting when you intentionally want255.

protips: Compare exported alpha values separately from perceived shine; the same numeric change does not prove the same brightness on every car.

articles.title: Reading a spec picture by colour
articles.summary: The combined spec image displays encoded material channels: red metallic, green roughness and blue clearcoat. It is not decorative paint RGB. Read the channel values separately; combined colours do not guarantee mirror reflections, matte paint or physical material percentages.
articles.what: Each RGB component is a material value in the8-bit spec image, not a body paint colour. High red indicates higher encoded metallic; green is encoded roughness; blue carries clearcoat. A nearly black RGB tuple has low channel values, which does not prove a matte material. A red-heavy tuple can represent high metallic with low roughness, but final reflection appearance also depends on clearcoat, source paint, strength, other material contributors, the car and lighting. A white RGB tuple has high values in all three channels, not white decorative paint. Ordinary export constraints may alter authored low values, so inspect the composed output as well as input.
when: You open a spec file in an image viewer and want to make sense of it
You compare two finishes and want to see what differs
how: Open MASK > Advanced spec utilities and choose Material Sampler, which opens the Spec Map Inspector.
Click ALL to see the combined map, or R, G, B and A to see one channel alone.
Use the Sample point to read exact numbers.
tips: Read metallic, roughness and clearcoat separately before diagnosing a combined colour.
pitfalls: Do not infer physical material fractions, exact gloss percentages or universal reflections from RGB labels.
A named finish selected by helper shorthand is not proof that an exact requested byte was written.

deep.heading: Source and composed values
deep.body: The channel tuple is a material representation. Strength, masks, weighted bases, spec overlays and final floors can change the composed values; a bare input number is not complete output evidence.

combos.why: Click a spot and read the exact bytes instead of guessing from colour.
Blue is backwards; the most common mis-reading.

faq.q: Does a red spec pixel guarantee perfect mirror reflections?
faq.a: No. It shows a red-heavy encoded material tuple, not a verified reflection outcome. Inspect green roughness, blue clearcoat, source paint and the composed material on the actual car. Metallic alone is not a perfect-mirror guarantee.

faq.q: Does a black spec pixel prove the paint is matte?
faq.a: No. A black RGB tuple means low encoded metallic, roughness and clearcoat, not a matte paint diagnosis. High roughness is what distinguishes a rougher material baseline; ordinary output constraints may also change low authored values.

faq.q: Does white in the combined spec preview mean white body paint?
faq.a: No. In the combined spec image white means high encoded R/G/B material values. Paint RGB is a separate image; judge source paint colour separately from its material response.

faq.q: Is the spec picture what iRacing shows?
faq.a: The simulator reads material channel values and lights the car; the combined RGB spec picture is a diagnostic representation, not a screenshot of the resulting painted car.

faq.q: What does g60 mean for a spec channel?
faq.a: If you mean the actual8-bit green channel,60 is the encoded roughness byte on a0–255 scale. It is not sixty percent gloss or paint brightness. This differs from the Offline Helper’s approximate shorthand interpretation; inspect any proposed operation instead of assuming it writes60 exactly.

faq.q: Is roughness50 the same as fifty percent glossy?
faq.a: No. An actual roughness byte50 is an encoded material value, not a measured percentage of gloss. A0–100 control, Spec Strength percentage and a typed helper shorthand can mean different things; confirm which field and the composed channel value.

faq.q: Does metal200 describe a physical percentage of metal in the car?
faq.a: No. An actual metallic byte200 is an encoded material-channel value on a0–255 scale, not measured physical composition. It also does not guarantee a particular shine, texture or paint transparency.

faq.q: Does red and green in my spec map mean the car paint will swap colours?
faq.a: No. Red and green in combined spec display metallic and roughness bytes, not two decorative paint colours to exchange. Paint RGB is separate. Inspect each channel and the composed result; swapping material bytes would change material meaning, not trade the corresponding paint colours.

faq.q: If I swap red and green spec channel bytes, am I swapping paint colours or material properties?
faq.a: You would change the material encoding: red bytes supply metallic and green bytes supply roughness. This is not exchanging red and green decorative paint. It can produce a very different material response, and final output constraints may modify values. This explanation does not claim an Offline command exists to perform a spec-channel swap.

articles.title: The metal and roughness grid
articles.summary: A metal/roughness grid describes material values at a pixel or region. A textured or stacked finish can occupy many points; clearcoat, paint and lighting still affect its appearance.
articles.what: Metallic and roughness are separate encoded material channels. A constant Foundation material can provide a useful starting point, while a patterned finish varies across pixels. An average point can hide smooth and rough regions or metallic and nonmetallic features. Clearcoat is a separate channel, and a material label is not a complete native appearance prediction.
when: You want to place a finish on a map of looks
You are building a custom look and need target numbers
how: Inspect metallic and roughness separately in the intended region.
Check clearcoat and the underlying paint alongside them.
Compare spatial variation rather than reducing every textured finish to one mean.

controls.label: R METAL
controls.effect: Moves the finish along the metal axis.

controls.label: G ROUGH
controls.effect: Moves the finish along the roughness axis.

tips: Foundation points (metal, roughness, coat): Gloss 0, 30, 16. Wet Look 0, 15, 16. Pearl 100, 40, 16. Metallic 200, 50, 16. Brushed 180, 75, 65. Satin Chrome 250, 45, 40. Chrome 255, 2, 16. Matte 0, 200, 160.
pitfalls: High metal with high roughness gives a chalky look, not a silver one.
Metal below 240 cannot go under roughness 15.

deep.heading: Spatial fields rather than one universal point
deep.body: The blend helpers accept arrays. Frost Etch can raise roughness while lowering metallic and clearcoat; Angle Flip can change metallic and coat while retaining roughness. Named material responses can therefore move different pixels in different directions. Numbers below or beyond final output limits can occur as intermediate values.

mistakes.symptom: My brushed look is just a flat grey metal.
mistakes.cause: Only the average values were set. Brushed needs variation in the spec.
mistakes.fix: Add a brushed spec overlay on top of Brushed 180, 75, 65.

mistakes.symptom: A roughness under 15 was changed back.
mistakes.cause: It was a non-chrome pixel, so the floor lifted it.
mistakes.fix: Raise metal to 240 or more if you want a true mirror.

protips: The grid is two-dimensional but a good finish uses a third dimension: variation. Flat points look like paint swatches, varied points look like materials.
Dark chrome (250, 15, 40) is the quickest way to a black mirror finish; the extra coat makes it less sharp than chrome.

articles.title: The three iron rules
articles.summary: Ordinary composition floors clearcoat at16 and roughness at15 below metal240. Recognized authored clearcoat and explicit pattern-spec preservation have exceptions; inspect the composed map rather than assuming all inputs are treated alike.
articles.what: In ordinary whole-car composition, clearcoat below16 is raised to16. Blue255 is allowed. Recognized authored-spec ownership preserves clearcoat at its affected pixels; explicit pattern-spec preservation also bypasses that clearcoat floor. Importing a file alone does not establish either condition. Ordinary roughness below15 is raised when metallic is below240, except explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels. Authored clearcoat preservation alone does not bypass the roughness rule. Alpha is a separate lighting/material channel, not a gloss or paint-colour control. The composed output, including masks and later adjustments, is the place to check actual values.
when: A slider will not go further than you expect
You edit a spec outside the app and need the safe limits
how: Stay inside the limits when you hand edit a spec map: blue at 16 or more.
Keep roughness at 15 or more unless metal is 240 or more.
Let the app handle alpha.
tips: The Spec Sculpt Lab always exports iron-safe maps.
pitfalls: A hand-edited blue value of 1 to 15 will look washed out in the sim.
Resizing a spec picture can create forbidden values. Re-render instead of resizing.
aliases: why does shokker change my spec values

deep.heading: Ordinary floors, with explicit exceptions
deep.body: The final composition assignment floors blue clearcoat at16 except recognized authored or pattern-spec-preserved pixels. It floors green roughness at15 below red metallic240 except pattern-spec-preserved pixels. The byte conversion clips material values to0..255. Those assignments explain an ordinary input becoming16 or15, but do not prove a universal rule across every later material/brush operation.

deep.heading: Import is not ownership
deep.body: A downloaded or hand-edited file is not automatically a recognized authored-spec set. The engine checks authored identity and pixel ownership, and separately marks explicit pattern material preservation. Inspect the selected import, masks and composed output before promising exact channels.

deep.heading: Material values are not paint colours
deep.body: Spec RGB stores material data. Blue0 is not black paint and blue255 is not blue paint. Changing material channels changes reflections and the lit impression while source paint may remain unchanged. Alpha belongs to the lighting/material response rather than gloss.

examples.title: The slider that stops
examples.goal: Understand why B COAT will not go glossier than 16.
examples.result: The result is clipped at 16. Nothing changes, because 16 is already the glossiest coat the app allows.

examples.title: Roughness cannot go under 15
examples.goal: See the roughness floor on a non-metal finish.
examples.result: Roughness stays at 15 because the pixel is not chrome tier. Only metal of 240 or more may go lower.

combos.why: The blue channel details behind rule one.
The Spec Sculpt Lab applies the same rules before it writes a file.
Slider shifts are clipped at 0, 15 and 16 before the final rules run.

faq.q: Can I turn the iron rules off?
faq.a: Ordinary output applies these floors automatically. Recognized authored and pattern-spec preservation are supported exceptions, not a generic floor-off switch. Check the composed map and exact selected source.

faq.q: Why is my chrome allowed roughness 2 but my gloss is not?
faq.a: In ordinary composition, roughness below15 is allowed at metallic240 or above. Below240 it is floored to15, except explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels. Authored clearcoat preservation alone does not bypass roughness flooring.

faq.q: Does a hand-edited spec file get checked?
faq.a: A file edited outside SPB is not changed by SPB until used in its workflow. Importing it does not automatically establish authored preservation; inspect the composed result and recognized source identity.

faq.q: Does the preview follow the same rules?
faq.a: Use the preview to compare the material, then inspect the composed or exported map when exact bytes matter. Do not infer exact export values from a slider offset or a paint preview.

faq.q: Does a downloaded spec file automatically bypass the clearcoat floor?
faq.a: No. Mere import does not establish recognized authored-spec ownership or explicit pattern-spec preservation. Ordinary composition floors clearcoat at16 unless the affected pixels meet one of those conditions.

faq.q: Can a preserved pattern keep roughness below15 on non-metal pixels?
faq.a: The final ordinary roughness-floor assignment exempts explicitly preserved pattern-spec pixels. This is a recognized preservation path, not a guarantee for any arbitrary pattern or imported file; inspect the actual composed result.

faq.q: Does preserving authored clearcoat also preserve roughness?
faq.a: Not by itself. Authored clearcoat ownership exempts clearcoat from its final floor. The final roughness assignment separately exempts pattern-spec-preserved pixels; ordinary non-chrome roughness can still be raised to15.

mistakes.symptom: My exact coat of 0 became 16.
mistakes.cause: Normal zones are floored at 16. Only imported specs and pattern-driven pixels keep 0.
mistakes.fix: Use coat 16 for the shiniest look, or import an authored spec if you really need coat off.

mistakes.symptom: A blend between a clear zone and a bare zone looks whitewashed.
mistakes.cause: The blend crossed coat 1 to 15.
mistakes.fix: Hard-edge the zone, or keep both sides at 16 or more.

mistakes.symptom: A roughness below 15 got lifted.
mistakes.cause: The pixel is not chrome tier.
mistakes.fix: Raise metal to 240 or more if you want a mirror there.

protips: The iron rules are a safety net, not a design tool. If a slider hits one, the look is telling you to change the base finish instead.
Resizing a spec picture in an editor can reintroduce illegal values. Re-render at 2048 instead.

articles.title: Paint and spec work together
articles.summary: Paint colours and spec material channels serve different jobs. Compare actual material contrast and readability; the combined spec image is not a complementary-colour paint palette.
articles.what: Paint RGB describes colour. Spec red, green and blue encode metallic, roughness and clearcoat. Choosing a spec image because its combined display colour is opposite the paint colour does not establish a suitable material. Contrasting adjacent paint colours or materials can be a design option; it is not a guaranteed best-looking recipe. Inspect each material channel, target coverage, source protection and the actual car before accepting the choice.
when: Your car looks flat even though the colours are right
You want to choose finishes for neighbouring zones
how: Choose a readable paint palette for the intended numbers, sponsors and body areas.
Select material values and textures separately from decorative colour; compare separate spec channels.
Treat a focal area and calmer neighbours as design options, then verify readability at useful distances on the actual car.
tips: Fine-detail pixel targets express the owner’s finish design intention; they are not calibrated millimetres or a native per-car acceptance result.
Changing reflections can alter perceived paint appearance even when a material operation leaves paint RGB untouched.
pitfalls: Combined spec RGB is material data, not decorative colour.
No universal warm-matte/cool-metal, chrome-paint shade or one-hero recipe is established by this audit.
aliases: why does my car look flat

deep.heading: Colour versus material evidence
deep.body: Keep paint-palette decisions separate from encoded M/R/Cc data. Finishes can contribute paint colour when permitted, while spec-only operations can change reflections without repainting pixels. Source inspection and design suggestions do not establish native lighting or readability on every car.

faq.q: Why does my bright colour look flat?
faq.a: Probably the shine is the same everywhere. Add a neighbour with the opposite shine.

faq.q: Does more saturation help?
faq.a: No. Contrast between neighbours helps. More saturation mostly muddies a spec.

faq.q: What goes behind numbers?
faq.a: A calm gloss, satin or matte with strong colour contrast. Avoid sparkle, strong patterns and colour-shifting finishes there.

faq.q: Chrome on the whole car?
faq.a: It is loud and shows every flaw. It works as a show-car statement, but accents and trim usually look better.

faq.q: I mixed three extra bases and their percentages add to more than100. Does that make the car paint brighter?
faq.a: Additional-base material weights are Spec Strength times feature coverage. When their sum exceeds1 at a pixel, they normalize proportionally and the primary material has no remaining weight there. This spec budget is not a paint-brightness rule; paint contributions have separate controls and do not inherit the same order-independent mixing guarantee.

mistakes.symptom: Everything is metallic and nothing stands out.
mistakes.cause: One shine used all over.
mistakes.fix: Choose a hero zone, then give the neighbours matte or satin.

mistakes.symptom: Black chrome looks like a black hole.
mistakes.cause: Very dark paint under high metal.
mistakes.fix: Use Dark Chrome 250, 15, 40, or lighten the paint a little.

mistakes.symptom: It looked great as a thumbnail and muddy on the car.
mistakes.cause: Mid-tone mud at thumbnail size stays mud on the car.
mistakes.fix: Judge on the car at a distance and on a sunny track.

protips: Test the contrast with the spec views off: if two zones are only different in shine, they will read the same in a dull photo and different in the sim.
Flat paint with chrome trim lines is the modern retro look; gloss everywhere is the showroom look.

articles.title: How base, pattern and spec combine in a zone
articles.summary: In every zone the base finish gives the starting paint and spec, the pattern adds shape on top, and the spec overlays add surface detail last.
articles.what: Think of a zone as a short stack. First the base finish sets colour and spec. Then a pattern, up to five per zone, is laid over the paint. Pattern spec amount, if set, also carries the pattern into the spec map. Then up to five spec overlays per base add surface detail only to the spec, with no colour change. Finally the spec sliders, strength and blends tune the end result. Zones with lower numbers win where they overlap. Spec Doctor (Material / Spec menu) checks the finished spec map for common mistakes.
when: You are not sure which control changes colour and which changes shine
Two settings seem to fight each other
how: Set the base finish and its colour first.
Add a pattern and set its paint mode, opacity and scale.
Add a spec overlay if you want texture without colour.
Finish with SPEC STRENGTH and the R, G and B sliders.

controls.label: SPEC STRENGTH
controls.effect: Fades the base spec toward neutral.

tips: Overlay mode for a pattern hides the base colour with the pattern own colours. Use Blend to keep the paint colour.
Spec overlays never change the colour, so they are the safe way to add texture to a colour you like.
pitfalls: A pattern with spec amount at 0 does not touch the spec map. This is on purpose.
The lower-numbered zone wins an overlap.

deep.heading: Step 1: which zone owns each pixel
deep.body: Every zone builds a mask from its colour match or drawn area, softened with a small blur (about 2 pixels) unless the zone has Hard Edge on, and Hard Edge is on by default in every zone. Zones are processed in list order and an earlier zone claims first: where two overlap, the lower number wins and the later one is cut back. A soft mask above 0.15 is hardened to full ownership. At the end a zone replaces the spec fully where its mask is above 0.5, blends linearly between 0.05 and 0.5, and leaves the spot alone below that. Paint is blended by the mask in the paint stack.

deep.heading: Step 2: the paint stack inside a zone
deep.body: In order: the base finish paint (skipped when the colour mode is Use source paint, so only the spec changes); the base colour mode (solid, gradient, finish colours); hue, saturation and brightness inside the mask (hue up to 180 degrees either way, skipped if all three are under half a percent); base scale placement; then BASE STRENGTH, which mixes the result over your original paint. Patterns come after Base Strength, so lowering it never dims a pattern. Last come the second to fifth base overlays.

deep.heading: Step 3: the spec stack inside a zone
deep.body: In order: the base finish spec; SPEC STRENGTH pulling metal toward 0, roughness toward 128 and coat toward 16; base scale, rotation and clear-coat quality; a second base blended through its gradient; spec patterns (metal, roughness and coat ticks); pattern spec amount; second to fifth base overlays; then the versioned spec overlays, applied last on the finished material as a mix toward their target. After the finish is built: an imported spec map if present, spec placement, then the three SPEC sliders (R, G, B), then Material Remap, Material Override and Lighting Mask, in that order.

deep.heading: Step 4: after every zone is done
deep.body: The app protects numbers and sponsors: wherever the decal mask is on, the original colour is restored so no overlay can repaint them. Wear is applied in one pass, scaled per zone. Decal spec finishes and spec stamps are blended in by their own alpha. Then the final floors run (coat at least 16, roughness at least 15 under metal 240) and the paint and spec files are written. Preview runs exactly the same steps at a smaller size.

examples.title: Pearl body with carbon hood stripes
examples.goal: Build a layered finish and predict each layer.

settings.Spec overlay: Brushed grain, M and R ticked, Strength 50

examples.result: Pearl shimmer on gloss, a carbon weave that keeps the body colour, grain only in the shine, and a slightly softer gloss from the slider at the end.

examples.title: Overlap on purpose
examples.goal: Make a stripe beat the body where they overlap.
examples.result: The stripe is higher in the list, so it keeps the overlap. Swap the order and the body wins.

combos.why: Step 3 ends with these three sliders.
Spec Strength sits at the start of Step 3 and Base Strength at the end of Step 2. They never touch each other.
The pattern layers that sit between the base and the overlays.

faq.q: Does Base Strength change the shine?
faq.a: No. Base Strength only blends the paint toward your original colours. SPEC STRENGTH changes the shine.

faq.q: Which zone wins when two overlap?
faq.a: The one higher in the list (lower number). + Add Zone puts the new zone at the bottom, so it loses overlaps until you drag it up; Chat and presets place new zones at the top.

faq.q: What runs last, my slider or my overlay?
faq.a: The overlays run first as part of the finish, then the R, G and B sliders, then Remap, Override and Lighting Mask.

faq.q: Does the preview match the export?
faq.a: It runs the same steps and floors at a smaller size, so very fine detail can look different from the full render.

mistakes.symptom: My pattern is not dimmed when I lower Base Strength.
mistakes.cause: Patterns are added after Base Strength.
mistakes.fix: Lower the pattern opacity instead.

mistakes.symptom: A zone changes nothing.
mistakes.cause: A higher zone covers it, the colour match selects nothing, or Base Strength or intensity is low.
mistakes.fix: Check the list order, then the zone mask, then the strength sliders.

mistakes.symptom: Sponsors got a chrome look.
mistakes.cause: The body zone also grabbed the sponsor layer, and decals take the material under them.
mistakes.fix: Limit the body zone to the car paint layer and use a decal spec finish for the sponsors.

protips: Quick triage order for any odd look: zone owner, then base colour mode, then Base Strength, then SPEC STRENGTH, then the sliders.

There are at most five pattern layers per zone and five spec overlays per base (each of a zone's five bases has its own stack), and each zone renders with its own random seed, so two zones with the same finish never repeat exactly.

articles.title: Colour space, files and preview truth
articles.summary: The paint file is an ordinary colour picture and the spec file is raw data. iRacing builds its own version from them, so a stale build can hide your newest file.
articles.what: Shokker Paint Booth writes two files per car: a 24-bit paint TGA and a 32-bit spec TGA with an alpha channel, both 2048 by 2048. The paint is read as normal screen colour. The spec is read as straight numbers, with no colour correction. That is why a pretty spec picture on screen only matters as data. iRacing then compiles the TGAs into a faster .mip file, and an old .mip can show instead of your new TGA until it is rebuilt.
when: Your car looks old in the sim after a fresh export
You open the spec TGA in an image editor
how: Export or deploy the car.
If the sim shows an old look, delete the stale .mip for that car so iRacing rebuilds it.
Never apply colour management or sharpening to a spec file.
tips: Judge finishes on the car preview or in the sim, not on the flat template.
The preview is a close guide, not a perfect copy of the sim shader.
pitfalls: Saving the spec through a photo editor can shift values and break the iron rules.
Wireframe and mask overlays in the preview can hide the real finish. Turn them off before judging.

deep.heading: Two files, two kinds of data
deep.body: The paint file is 24-bit colour, read as normal screen colour. The spec file is 32-bit with alpha and is read as raw numbers, with no colour correction. Both are 2048 by 2048 for a standard car, and the size must match the car template exactly, or iRacing shows the paint shop colours instead. An optional normal map can be written from the metal channel.

deep.heading: The compiled copy trap
deep.body: The first time iRacing loads your files it compiles the spec into a faster copy next to it. If you render again and the look does not change, that compiled copy is stale. Press Ctrl+R in the sim to reload the car textures. If the old shine still shows, move that car's compiled spec copy out of the folder and reload. Other drivers only see your spec if the compiled copy is shared too; Trading Paints shares it.

deep.heading: Byte order and tools
deep.body: The spec file stores its bytes as blue, green, red, alpha, while tools show red, green, blue, alpha. That is normal, so never swap channels by hand. Saving the spec through a photo editor can shift values, apply colour management or sharpen edges, all of which break the iron rules.

examples.title: Spec change not visible
examples.goal: Make a new render show up in the sim.

settings.If still old: Move the compiled spec copy for that car out of the folder, then Ctrl+R again

examples.result: iRacing rebuilds the compiled copy from the new spec and shows the new shine.

examples.title: Paint all black
examples.goal: Fix a paint file that loads wrong.
examples.result: The paint loads with its real colours.

combos.why: The 32-bit spec file is the one with alpha.
Editing the file elsewhere can break the rules the app enforces.

faq.q: How big must the paint be?
faq.a: Exactly 2048 by 2048 (or 1024 by 1024), 24-bit.

faq.q: Why do other drivers not see my shine?
faq.a: iRacing never shares textures. Files must be in their folder; Trading Paints does that, and its spec needs the compiled copy.

faq.q: Why is my paint all black?
faq.a: It was saved with the template alpha channel instead of 24-bit, or 2048 paint textures is off in the sim.

faq.q: Do I need the spec file at all?
faq.a: No. Without it iRacing uses the car normal material. Your colours still show.

mistakes.symptom: New shine does not show after a render.
mistakes.cause: A stale compiled copy.
mistakes.fix: Ctrl+R in the sim, or move the compiled copy out and reload.

mistakes.symptom: iRacing shows paint shop colours.
mistakes.cause: Wrong size.
mistakes.fix: Use the car template size exactly and never resize.

protips: In a replay, reload textures at a moment when the car is not in the pit stall.
A render takes seconds to about a minute. If it takes much longer, check how many zones have their own painted area.

articles.title: Spec strength and independent spec
articles.summary: SPEC STRENGTH moves an ordinary base toward M/R/CC 0/128/16, not always toward less shine: rough Matte becomes smoother as strength falls. It changes material rather than paint contribution; overlays can remain at base strength0. BASE STRENGTH is a separate paint control. Per-Zone imported source strength is a different weight: at zero, its source blend uses neutral material and still applies generated RGB material deltas, so it does not automatically disable the Base.
articles.what: SPEC STRENGTH adjusts the base material response, separately from BASE STRENGTH, which controls the paint contribution. In the ordinary base path, lowering spec strength moves metallic toward0, roughness toward128 and clearcoat toward16. This is not a universal less-shiny slider: rough materials above128 become smoother as it falls, while very smooth materials become rougher. At0 the base reaches the neutral starting values0/128/16; it does not erase the whole spec map, and overlays or later adjustments can still contribute. Recognized authored spec imports bypass ordinary material-strength scaling to preserve their channels. INDEPENDENT SPEC unlocks SPEC SCALE for a separate material texture size; SPEC ROTATION is separately available.
when: A finish is too loud and you want it calmer
You want the shine texture to run in a different direction from the paint
how: Open the zone and find SPEC STRENGTH. Drag it in steps of 5.
Tick the INDEPENDENT SPEC box in the Spec Scale row to unlock SPEC SCALE. SPEC ROTATION is always live.
Render and compare.

controls.label: SPEC STRENGTH
controls.effect: Scales metal, roughness and coat toward neutral.

controls.label: INDEPENDENT SPEC
controls.effect: Frees spec scale and rotation from the base.

tips: Behind the slider: metal times strength, roughness moves toward 128 and coat toward 16.
pitfalls: Strength 0 is neutral, not dull: coat goes to 16, the glossiest value.
Spec strength does not change colour.
aliases: which slider makes the car less shiny
material size separately from paint size

deep.heading: Strength is a movement toward neutral
deep.body: The ordinary base interpolation is channel-by-channel: M approaches0, R approaches128, CC approaches16. At50percent the flat Matte starting material becomes0/164/88 before composition; lowering its roughness makes it smoother. A Chrome starting material becomes127.5/65/16, losing metallic response and its sharp mirror. Different materials therefore change in different directions.

deep.heading: Separate paint, base material and overlay controls
deep.body: BASE STRENGTH belongs to paint contribution. SPEC STRENGTH belongs to the base material response. Overlay stacks and additional bases have their own contribution and later composition. Use source paint to retain artwork when intended; source-colour preservation is separate from protecting sponsor material.

examples.title: Half-chrome
examples.goal: A softer chrome look without changing finish.
examples.result: Metal about 128 and roughness about 65: a bright metallic with soft reflections instead of a mirror.

examples.title: Grain across the paint grain
examples.goal: Turn the shine texture 45 degrees from the paint texture.
examples.result: The spec grain is finer and diagonal to the base texture.

combos.why: The two controls that Independent Spec unlocks.
Where Spec Strength sits in the order of operations.
Sliders add after strength; use strength for overall, sliders for one channel.

faq.q: When independent spec is disabled does it use the base current scale?
faq.a: If you mean INDEPENDENT SPEC for scale, yes: disabling it matches the current BASE SCALE again. Spec Strength is a different control; it changes material values rather than texture size.

faq.q: Does strength 0 mean dull?
faq.a: No. In the ordinary base path,0 moves the base material to M/R/CC 0/128/16. That is a neutral starting response, not a guarantee of dullness or absence of reflections. Overlays, other bases and later adjustments can still affect the final spec.

faq.q: Which slider makes the car less shiny?
faq.a: For broader, less sharp reflections, inspect green roughness and raise it when appropriate. Lowering SPEC STRENGTH is not always less shiny: it moves roughness toward128, so a rough Matte base can become smoother. Compare all material channels and the composed map.

faq.q: Does strength change colour?
faq.a: SPEC STRENGTH targets the base material channels rather than repainting your source. Its changed reflections can still alter the visible impression of colour. BASE STRENGTH and BASE COLOR are separate paint choices; recognized authored specs have a preservation exception.

faq.q: Why can I not change SPEC SCALE?
faq.a: It is locked until INDEPENDENT SPEC is ticked.

faq.q: What is the difference between BASE STRENGTH and SPEC STRENGTH?
faq.a: BASE STRENGTH controls the base paint contribution; SPEC STRENGTH controls its material response in the ordinary path. To preserve artwork, inspect BASE COLOR too: choose Use source paint (spec only) when intended. Lowering one strength does not automatically turn off the other.

faq.q: Why does lowering spec strength make my matte finish shinier?
faq.a: The ordinary base roughness moves toward128. Matte starts at200, so reducing strength makes its base roughness lower and the surface smoother; its clearcoat also moves toward16. Use green roughness and the composed spec to diagnose the result rather than treating spec strength as a less-shiny slider.

faq.q: Does spec strength zero disable all spec overlays?
faq.a: No. It neutralizes the ordinary base response toward0/128/16, not the entire spec composition. Spec overlays, additional bases and later channel adjustments may still contribute. Mute overlays separately and compare the spec views.

faq.q: What are Chrome and Matte at fifty percent spec strength?
faq.a: For the ordinary plain base scaling step, Chrome255/2/16 becomes127.5/65/16; Matte0/200/160 becomes0/164/88. These are intermediate values before byte conversion, floors, masks and other effects, not guaranteed final export bytes.

faq.q: Why does spec strength not change my authored spec import?
faq.a: The recognized authored-spec path deliberately bypasses ordinary base strength scaling to preserve uploaded material channels. A file import alone does not prove that classification. Inspect the selected import and composed result; do not assume a broken slider.

faq.q: Will reducing spec strength preserve my sponsor material?
faq.a: No automatic sponsor protection is implied. It changes the base material where the zone applies. Keep source paint when intended and target or protect sponsor and number material separately; inspect masks and layer restrictions before applying changes.

faq.q: Why does spec scale do nothing on a plain Foundation material?
faq.a: A plain Foundation material has constant base-spec channels, so there is no grain or flake texture for scaling to resize. INDEPENDENT SPEC unlocks the scale control, but it cannot create texture. A separate textured material or spec overlay is needed for visible detail.

faq.q: Does strength0 mean the entire spec file is blank?
faq.a: No. Ordinary base spec strength0 gives neutral base M/R/CC 0/128/16, not a blank or deleted spec file. Overlays, other bases and adjustments can still affect the composed map.

faq.q: Does strength0 mean dull?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Spec strength0 neutralizes the ordinary base to0/128/16. It is not a universal dullness setting: lowering strength can make a rough base smoother, and overlays or later adjustments still contribute.

faq.q: Can I adjust material size separately from paint size?
faq.a: Yes: INDEPENDENT SPEC unlocks SPEC SCALE separately from base paint scale. It adjusts an existing material texture, not the output image resolution. A plain Foundation base has constant channels, so scaling it does not create visible grain.

faq.q: Is reduced lighting exactly fifty percent as bright on all cars?
faq.a: No such brightness guarantee was measured. Reduced Lighting writes alpha128, while Spec Strength is a different control for M/R/C. The simulator’s lighting/material response determines perceived brightness; a numeric midpoint does not prove half the visible brightness.

faq.q: I want a fine finish effect rather than big blobs. Should I reduce strength or adjust its material scale first?
faq.a: Use the relevant scale/placement controls to change feature size, and inspect the actual result. Spec Strength changes material contribution rather than geometry. Base/Spec scales are linked by default; independent Spec Scale separates the material path when appropriate. Paint colour scale and finish-specific generators have their own behavior, so no single numeric scale is a universal fine-detail recommendation.

mistakes.symptom: Lowering strength made the car look like plain gloss.
mistakes.cause: Strength pulls toward a neutral plate, so every finish converges on plain gloss at 0.
mistakes.fix: Lower in small steps, or change the base finish.

mistakes.symptom: I used strength to shrink a pattern.
mistakes.cause: Strength is not size.
mistakes.fix: Use scale. Smaller number means finer and more repeats.

protips: Authored imports (SHOKK DROP sets) ignore SPEC STRENGTH on purpose, so their hand-tuned numbers stay exact.
The same slider also scales the noise in noisy bases, so on those the effect is a bit stronger than the plain formula.

articles.title: Spec scale and rotation
articles.summary: To change material texture spacing or shine-detail size while keeping paint placement, enable Independent Spec and adjust Spec Scale for the selected zone. The material needs existing texture; scaling plain constant Satin does not create grain. Turning independence off matches the current Base Scale again. Source pixel periods are not calibrated physical dimensions on a car; inspect the specific template and placement rather than assuming equal feature sizes across car types.
articles.what: Material spacing, shine-detail size and surface texture size are useful ways to describe SPEC SCALE: it transforms existing material detail rather than resizing artwork. Paint placement and material placement are separate when Independent Spec is enabled. SPEC SCALE follows BASE SCALE until its mode is independent. In the active primary-base link its range is 0.05 to 5.00 in 0.05 steps. Enabling independence starts from the currently linked scale; later BASE SCALE changes leave that independent spec scale alone. Returning to match mode resumes the current base scale. These controls transform existing spec detail; they do not invent grain in a constant material. Ordinary Foundation Brushed, Metallic and the other 20 plain materials start with constant spec values. A textured finish or a suitable spec overlay is needed for actual grain.

A weave or flake needs to be finer

deep.title: Spec scale and rotation
deep.body: SPEC SCALE follows BASE SCALE until its mode is independent. In the active primary-base link its range is 0.05 to 5.00 in 0.05 steps. Enabling independence starts from the currently linked scale; later BASE SCALE changes leave that independent spec scale alone. Returning to match mode resumes the current base scale. A textured finish or a suitable spec overlay is needed for actual grain.

faq.q: If I unlink spec scale, will the next base scale change drag it along?
faq.a: No. Once spec scale is independent, changing BASE SCALE leaves it alone. Turn independent mode off to match the current BASE SCALE again.

faq.q: Does reset spec scale put it back to 1.00?
faq.a: No. Reset Spec Scale returns to match mode at the current BASE SCALE, which may be different from 1.00.

faq.q: Can I make the spec texture smaller without changing my paint?
faq.a: Yes: enable INDEPENDENT SPEC and adjust SPEC SCALE for the selected zone. This changes spec placement without changing the paint-scale setting; the material must contain texture to show a size change.

faq.q: Why does changing Spec Scale not add grain to Foundation Brushed?
faq.a: Plain Foundation Brushed uses constant M/R/CC material values. Scale cannot invent grain; use a finish or spec overlay that actually generates texture.

faq.q: Does lowering Spec Strength make flakes smaller?
faq.a: No. Strength changes material values toward neutral, not feature size. Use the scale control belonging to the source of the flakes; constant materials have no flake pattern to resize.

faq.q: What happens when I turn Independent Spec off?
faq.a: Spec scale matches the current BASE SCALE again. Turning independence on initially preserves that linked value, then allows spec scale to vary separately.

faq.q: Does resetting Spec Scale always restore one?
faq.a: No. The current Reset Spec Scale handler returns it to match mode at the current BASE SCALE. Align Spec to Base also copies base rotation.

faq.q: Does rotation create texture on a flat material?
faq.a: No. A constant material has nothing internal to turn. Rotation changes existing material detail, not its construction.

faq.q: Can I change just the woven material spacing and keep the coloured design where it is?
faq.a: Enable Independent Spec for the selected zone, then adjust Spec Scale. This separates material placement from the base paint-scale setting. The material must contain woven detail; a plain constant material has none to resize. If you want the original artwork rather than the finish palette, check Use source paint for the ordinary primary-base path too. Other paint contributors and target masks remain separate checks.

faq.q: If I turn independent spec off, does the shine scale go back to 1 or match my base?
faq.a: It matches the current Base Scale, which need not be 1.00. Turning independence on starts from that linked value, then allows material scale to change separately.

faq.q: My finish is plain satin. Can lowering scale add fine grain?
faq.a: Plain Foundation Satin starts with constant material channels. Scale can resize existing detail but cannot create grain. Choose a textured material or spec overlay if grain is intended; keep colour mode and artwork protection separate.

faq.q: A finish says20pixel cells. Does that prove the pattern is the same physical size on my stock car and formula car?
faq.a: No. A source cell size describes image coordinates, not physical car dimensions. Template mapping, output resolution and placement/scaling can change how features sit on different cars. Inspect the correct template and simulator; no millimetre measurement or uniform cross-car geometry was established.

articles.title: R, G and B channel sliders
articles.summary: The R METAL, G ROUGH and B COAT sliders nudge the finish spec. They add or subtract under the zone and then the app clips to safe limits.
articles.what: These three sliders shift each channel by up to 127 either way, in steps of 5. The shift is added to the finish spec under the zone shape, then clipped at the floors: 0 for metal, 15 for roughness and 16 for coat. They are the fine-tuning tool after you pick a finish. The built-in Feels set them in one click.
when: A finish is almost right but a touch too dull or too rough
You want a consistent tweak across several zones
how: Open the zone editor, go to the BASE section and find Spec Sliders.
Move R METAL, G ROUGH and B COAT.
Use the Feel picker or the save icon for presets.

controls.label: G ROUGH

controls.label: B COAT

tips: For a wetter look, lower G ROUGH, and lower B COAT if the finish coat is above 16.
The B COAT slider tooltip in the app says higher is a stronger mirror. The number is really added to the coat value, where bigger means duller, so judge by eye in the preview.
pitfalls: Shifts that reach a floor stop having an effect.
Large shifts can cancel the finish character.

actions.label: Spec Sliders (R Metal, G Rough, B Coat)

deep.heading: Exactly what a slider does
deep.body: Each slider adds its value, from minus 127 to plus 127, to that channel under the zone mask. The result is clipped at 0 to 255, with floors of 0 for metal, 15 for roughness and 16 for coat. Sliders at 0 (or all under half a point) are ignored. The sliders run after patterns, overlays and blend modes, so they are the last creative step; only Remap, Override and Lighting Mask come after.

deep.heading: Which way each one goes
deep.body: Metal plus means more metal. Roughness plus means duller, minus means glossier. Coat plus means duller, because blue is backwards, minus means glossier and stops at 16. Rough recipes: satin from gloss is G ROUGH plus 40 to plus 80 with B COAT plus 30 to plus 60. Wetter is G ROUGH minus and B COAT minus.

deep.heading: Sliders versus other tools
deep.body: Sliders shift a whole zone evenly. Material Remap squeezes a channel into a new low to high range and keeps variation. Material Override sets flat values. Spec Strength pulls everything toward neutral. A shift of 20 is subtle, 50 is a clear style change, and anything near 100 usually cancels the finish character.

examples.goal: Take a gloss body to satin without changing the base.
examples.result: Roughness around 90 and coat around 61: a quiet satin.

examples.title: Duller candy

examples.result: Roughness 45 and coat 36: the candy colour stays but the glassy look relaxes into a satin candy.
